text:
**Keep the Join: Why Primary Schools Should Still Teach Joined-Up Handwriting**

Every few years, someone declares handwriting dead. The keyboard has won, the argument goes, and children should not spend precious hours looping their l's and crossing their t's when they will spend their working lives tapping on glass. It is a tidy argument. It is also wrong, and primary schools should keep teaching joined-up handwriting.

Start with what the case against actually claims. It rests on three pillars. First, that typing is the skill of the future. Second, that cursive is slow to master and crowds out other learning. Third, that plenty of adults print or mix styles anyway, so the joined form is a relic. Each of these contains a grain of truth. None survives a closer look.

Take the claim about the future. Children do need to type, and they need to type well. Nobody serious argues otherwise. But the choice is a false one. A school day is not a zero-sum contest between pens and keyboards, and a child who learns to write by hand is not thereby prevented from learning to type. Most of us did both. The question is whether handwriting still does something that typing does not. The evidence suggests it does.

Researchers who study how the brain learns to read have found that forming letters by hand engages the brain differently from pressing keys. In one well-known line of work, young children who learned letters by writing them showed stronger activation in reading-related brain regions than those who typed or traced them. Studies of note-taking point the same way. Students who write notes by hand tend to process and reword what they hear, because they cannot keep pace with a lecturer word for word. Typists, who can, often transcribe without thinking. The slowness of the pen is, in this case, a feature. It forces selection, and selection is where understanding happens.

None of this research is a magic wand, and some of it is contested. Sample sizes are small. Not every study separates joined writing from printed writing. An honest advocate should say so. But the weight of the findings leans one way, and a school system deciding whether to discard a centuries-old skill ought to ask for strong evidence that the discard is safe. That evidence does not exist. Those who want to drop cursive are the ones making the bold claim, and they have not met their burden.

Now consider the second pillar, that joined writing is too slow to learn. The opposite is closer to the truth. Joined-up writing exists because it is faster and smoother. When a child prints, the pen lifts after every letter. Each lift is a small decision, a restart, a chance to reverse a b and a d. In a joined script, the hand moves in a continuous flow and a word becomes a single gesture. Many teachers who favour early cursive report that the reversal problem shrinks, because the entry stroke gives each letter only one natural way to begin. Children with dyslexia and dyspraxia are often cited here. For some of them, the rhythm of a joined hand helps. For others it does not, and a good teacher adapts. That is a case for flexibility, not abolition.

Speed matters beyond neatness. Fluent handwriting frees a child's attention. A pupil who must concentrate on forming each letter has less mental room left for spelling, grammar and ideas. Once the movement is automatic, the mind is released to think about what to say. This is why handwriting fluency in the early years predicts the quality of later written composition. A child who struggles to get words onto the page will write fewer of them, and shorter ones, and will come to dislike writing. Teaching a fast, efficient hand early is an investment in everything that follows.

The third pillar, that adults abandon cursive anyway, proves less than it seems. Of course adults develop their own hands. Almost nobody writes the way the copybook taught them. But that is how every skill matures. We learn a standard form so that we can depart from it with some awareness. Adults who write quickly tend to drift toward a semi-joined hybrid, linking the letter pairs that flow naturally and lifting the pen where it does not. That is precisely the style that a joined-up curriculum produces by design. The adult hybrid is not evidence against teaching cursive. It is the destination, and a systematic early start is the most reliable road there.

There is also a plain practical point. People still write by hand, constantly. They sign forms, jot shopping lists, fill in cards, leave notes on fridges, annotate documents, take quick notes in meetings where a laptop would feel rude. Pupils sit examinations in which they must write for hours, by hand, at speed, legibly. A child who cannot write fast and clearly is penalised at the exact moments that matter most to them. Printing at exam pace is cramped and tiring. A fluent joined hand is less so. If we care about fairness, we should care that every child leaves primary school able to write comfortably, not only those whose parents taught them at home.

That last point deserves emphasis, because it is where the argument becomes about equity. If schools stop teaching handwriting systematically, the skill does not vanish. It simply stops being taught to those who cannot get it elsewhere. Children from families with time, books and a tradition of writing letters will still learn to write well. Others will not. The result is a quiet widening of an advantage that schools exist to narrow.

Then there is the matter of reading. Joined-up script is the way a great deal of the written world looks. Old letters, family records, historical documents, handwritten recipes, a grandparent's birthday card: all of it arrives in cursive. A child who cannot read it is cut off from a stretch of their own past. That sounds sentimental, and perhaps it is, but culture is partly made of such continuities. Teaching a child to read and write a handwritten script costs a modest number of lessons. Losing it costs a generation's access to the handwriting of the one before.

I do not want to overstate the case. A handwriting curriculum can be done badly. Some schools drill it joylessly, mark children down for slanting the wrong way, and treat neatness as a moral quality. That is a mistake. The goal is legibility and fluency, not calligraphy. Children should not be made to feel that their worth depends on the shape of a lowercase g. Nor should handwriting steal time from reading, mathematics or play. Ten minutes a day of short, focused practice, ideally woven into real writing, is enough. And teachers should be free to adapt for the child with motor difficulties, the left-hander, the pupil for whom a different approach works better. Rigidity serves nobody.

Nor should anyone pretend that a particular style, whether a looped one, a pre-cursive one with exit flicks, or a purely italic one, is sacred. Schools can choose a script that suits them. What matters is that they choose one, teach it well, and move children toward a fluent joined hand by the upper primary years.

The strongest version of the opposing view is a humble one: perhaps handwriting is simply less important than it was, and the time is better spent elsewhere. This deserves a straight answer. It is true that handwriting matters less than it did in 1950. It does not follow that it matters little. The skill is cheap to teach, durable once learned, and useful in ways that are easy to overlook until they are missing. It supports reading, composition, memory and examination performance. It costs a few minutes a day. Few other parts of the primary curriculum offer so much for so little.

When a technology arrives that can do a job better, we are right to ask whether the old way is still worth keeping. Sometimes it is not. Nobody mourns the slide rule. But handwriting is not a slide rule. It is not merely a way of producing text. It is a way of thinking, a motor skill tied up with how children learn language, and a means of personal expression that no font quite replicates. A keyboard gives every child the same letters. A pen gives each child their own.

So teach the join. Teach it briefly, kindly and well. Teach it alongside typing, not instead of it. And resist the temptation to treat a skill as obsolete simply because it is old. The children in our classrooms will type for most of their lives. They will also, at some point, need to write a note by hand, sign their name, or read what someone wrote to them long ago. Let them do all of it with confidence.
